messages.author: 69658a5d047f38b4
messages.subject: New package(s)
parts:
Hi again,

Since Hadley laid down the path for externalization of components of ggplot in 0.9, I thought I would take a stab at my first R package and start a collection of fortify and autoplot functions. I currently have a few things ready in:
https://gitorious.org/r/multivariate-ggplot/trees/master
https://gitorious.org/r/bayes-ggplot/trees/master
(yes I'll move to github ;) ) and I am currently working on similar stuff for quantile regression.

A few questions to knowledgeable people before I start:

- would you group fortify methods with autoplot methods (autoplot being targeted at plotting the output from fortify) and would you make two packages (since fortify has a use on its own)?

- what about the name(s): autoplot does not sound vey ggplot-ish, especially compared to ggstructure, ggorder and all the rest. autoggplot? ggauto?

- in many cases, there are several plots one would want to inspect automatically (observations and variables in factorial analysis, fit and residuals structure in a linear model etc.). What is the behaviour you would prefer:
. sequential plots (like with plot.lm() )
. several plotting windows (like what FactoMineR does if you know this package)
. juxtaposed plots (with viewports etc.)
The argument to chose which plots to produce will likely be `plot` rather than `which` (`which` is used in plot.lm, I find it cryptic but maybe that's just a language problem).

Other than that:
I think I'll try to use roxygen2 for the documentation and test_that for the tests, so everyone here should feel at home.
I'll probably split all functions in their own file (see https://gitorious.org/r/multivariate-ggplot/blobs/master/autoplot-fact.R where everything is in one file).

Any advice you could give me would be useful. Thanks in advance,

Jean-Olivier Irisson

I am also (slowly) working on my first R package, an extension using
fortify/autoplot to make Kaplan-Meier curves from survfit objects from
the survival package. It also has older versions that use
as.data.frame/ggplot, though not as nicely.
> A few questions to knowledgeable people before I start:

My knowledge comes from what I've learned making this package, some
off-list discussions, and this older thread on the ggplot list
(ggplot-dev didn't exist then)
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/66883404b8163e0b

> - would you group fortify methods with autoplot methods (autoplot
> being targeted at plotting the output from fortify) and would you
> make two packages (since fortify has a use on its own)?

I would put them in the same package. I think of fortify as a mechanism
to get data from a specific data structure designed by someone else for
a particular purpose into a data.frame (*) since data.frames are what
ggplot2 works with. That is, I think of fortify as a gluing layer and
as such does not have much utility outside of ggplot/autoplot.

(*) Or at least a data.frame adorned with attributes that carry other
useful information, including other data frames.

That said, fortify is distinct enough in purpose that it should be a
separate function (and not just part of autoplot).

> - what about the name(s): autoplot does not sound vey ggplot-ish,
> especially compared to ggstructure, ggorder and all the rest.
> autoggplot? ggauto?

The name was suggested by Hadley (see a comment to the question at
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7098830/bad-idea-ggplotting-an-s3-class-object
) which is what I went with when I created the function (
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/286 and the requests it references).

> - in many cases, there are several plots one would want to inspect
> automatically (observations and variables in factorial analysis, fit
> and residuals structure in a linear model etc.). What is the
> behaviour you would prefer:
> . sequential plots (like with plot.lm() )
> . several plotting windows (like what FactoMineR does if you know this package)
> . juxtaposed plots (with viewports etc.)
> The argument to chose which plots to produce will likely be `plot`
> rather than `which` (`which` is used in plot.lm, I find it cryptic
> but maybe that's just a language problem).

The advantage of the sequential plots like plot.lm() is that you can
then wrap them in a par(mcol=c(2,2)) to get them all displayed together
easily. Generalizing that idea, maybe return a list of ggplot objects?
Printing the list will plot all in succession (where par(ask) (?) would
make it stop between). Also, a list of plots would be close to what
ggExtra:align.plots (or whatever its successor will be) takes, giving
the tiling ability. This gives your third option suggests, without much
work.

I'm ambivalent as to the argument name. I understand which in the
context of an index (effectively a subscript), but plot would be fine
too. Maybe have it take either a numeric index or a string which names
the plots, briefly.

> Other than that: I think I'll try to use roxygen2 for the
> documentation and test_that for the tests, so everyone here should
> feel at home. I'll probably split all functions in their own file
> (see
> https://gitorious.org/r/multivariate-ggplot/blobs/master/autoplot-fact.R
> where everything is in one file).

Yeah, roxygen2 and testthat are good. Basically, the full Wickhamsonian
approach. Throw a vignette in while you are at it :)

> Any advice you could give me would be useful.
> Thanks in advance,

OK about returning a list. That's what I did with autoplot.PCA/CA and such, but I could not find a good way to get them to plot separately. par(ask=T) is the answer but that would require the user to explicitly set it.

What about having, at the end of the function:

plots = list(first=p1, second=p2, third=p3)
par(ask=T)
print(plots)
par(ask=F)

return(invisible(plots))

that way the plots are printed, sequentially, but also returned in case the user what to continue modifying one of them.

About Hadley's suggestion: you would compute all plots every time and then let the user deal with which ones are plotted? I thought I would make things a bit more automated, since autoplot is likely to interest and audience less advanced in ggplot .

re displaying a list of plots, when I recently added marrangeGrob in
gridExtra, I defined the following print method,

function (x, ...)
lapply(x, function(.x) {
if (dev.interactive())
dev.new()
else grid.newpage()
grid.draw(.x)
}, ...)

so that an interactive session sees multiple pages (devAskNewPage()
could be inserted there instead), but non-interactive devices like
pdf, png, etc. produce multiple pages of output (bearing in mind that
for some formats you'll need to pass an incremental name like
Rplot%2d.png). It's also compatible with ggsave and grid.arrange.

Cheers,

baptiste

On 2012-Jan-23, at 23:50 , Brian Diggs wrote:
>
> My knowledge comes from what I've learned making this package, some off-list discussions, and this older thread on the ggplot list (ggplot-dev didn't exist then) http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/66883404b8163e0b

Thanks for the pointer and the wiki page. It's helpful.

To give my opinion on a few of the open questions:

- how to return things when a data.frame is not enough? This is the case for PCA where you typically have the coordinates of the objects and the coordinates of the variables. I decided, in concert with Hadley to use a named list of data.frames. It seems like the only logical solution in this case. Putting everything in a single data.frame does not make sense and there's not one data.frame that's more relevant than the other so putting one of the two as attribute would be meaningless. I feel that the list would be the best solution in most cases.

- names and methods: the package name will be autoplot and all fortify and autoplot methods will be exported (to make it easy to look at the code, which is essential if you want to tweak the plot further)

- extends vs depends: in the case of the special package with only fortify/autoplot methods, it will depend on ggplot. In the case of a few methods defined for special object in the specialized package, I would lean towards extends/recommends ggplot rather than explicitly depend on it, since it is likely than default plot methods will also exist.

I added a best practice which I think is essential:

`autoplot` should define default aesthetic mappings but allow the user to override them. One way to do it is to have a `mapping` argument to autoplot and then define the actual mapping as:

map <- c(mapping, aes_string(x="nameOfX", y="nameOfY", colour="nameOfColour"))
ggplot() + geom_foo(mapping=map)

for example.
> Yeah, roxygen2 and testthat are good. Basically, the full Wickhamsonian approach. Throw a vignette in while you are at it :)

"Wickhamsonian" indeed! I find myself writing this at the top of every R file I write:

library("plyr")
library("reshape")
library("ggplot2")
library("stringr")

I'm not using R anymore, I'm using HadlR ;)

parts: Regarding this question:

On 2012-Jan-24, at 10:33 , Jean-Olivier Irisson wrote:
>
> - how to return things when a data.frame is not enough? This is the case for PCA where you typically have the coordinates of the objects and the coordinates of the variables. I decided, in concert with Hadley to use a named list of data.frames. It seems like the only logical solution in this case. Putting everything in a single data.frame does not make sense and there's not one data.frame that's more relevant than the other so putting one of the two as attribute would be meaningless. I feel that the list would be the best solution in most cases.

I eventually changed my mind and made fortify return only one data.frame, with an addition argument type for the type of data that it returns (observations or variables in the case of a PCA). I think that's cleaner and more efficient (not both have to be extracted every time).

This way, the following autoplot functions do not have to adapt themselves to the fact that fortify produces a list and it allows to use the fortify methods inside a ggplot() call too. Indeed, extra arguments to ggplot() are passed to fortify so

pca <- prcomp(USArrests)
ggplot(pca) + geom_point(aes(x=.PC1, y=.PC2))
ggplot(pca, type="var") + geom_point(aes(x=.PC1, y=.PC2))

all work.

Minor suggestion, I think you want "||" in your condition. Also, to
make this work with ggsave, you'll need to make "ggplot_list" inherit
from "ggplot" so that ggsave is fooled into thinking that it's saving
a ggplot.


l = list(qplot(1,1, main="1"),
qplot(1,1, main="2"),
qplot(1,1, main="3"))
class(l) <- c("ggplot_list", "ggplot", class(l))

print(l)

ggsave("multipage.pdf", l)
ggsave("multipage%03d.png", l)

ggsave could also become a bit more general, and its return message
would indicate how many pages were saved, etc.

Cheers,

I ran a pcaMethods::pca() this morning using NIPALS, pareto scaling and mean centering. 

ggplot(PCA, type="var") + geom_point(aes(x=.PC1, y=.PC2))

Worked like a charm. The only thing I'm not quite seeing is how to use the various factors from the original dataframe. I think this is a problem with pcaMethods though. Like you need to be able to run the pca on a subset of columns and then reappend the PCA results as new columns to the orginal dataset. 

For example, the data I'm working is looking at color in fruit. The pca is run on metabolites and I'm outputting the color of the point using scale_color_identity(). If I supply pca() with the subset of the data (metabolites only) I lose the color information.

On 2012-Jul-07, at 10:13 , Brandon Hurr wrote:
>
> I ran a pcaMethods::pca() this morning using NIPALS, pareto scaling and mean centering.
> ggplot(PCA, type="var") + geom_point(aes(x=.PC1, y=.PC2))
>
> Worked like a charm. The only thing I'm not quite seeing is how to use the various factors from the original dataframe. I think this is a problem with pcaMethods though. Like you need to be able to run the pca on a subset of columns and then reappend the PCA results as new columns to the orginal dataset.
>
> For example, the data I'm working is looking at color in fruit. The pca is run on metabolites and I'm outputting the color of the point using scale_color_identity(). If I supply pca() with the subset of the data (metabolites only) I lose the color information.

That works by supplying the original data as the data argument to fortify(). Here is an example:

d <- data.frame(a=runif(10), b=runif(10), c=runif(10), foo=letters[round(runif(10, 1, 3))], bar=runif(10))

library("pcaMethods")
pca <- pca(d[,1:3], method="nipals", scale="pareto")
# the active variables are a, b and c only

# get the latest version, I changed stuff a few minutes ago
install_github("autoplot", "jiho")

library("autoplot")
# by default, pca() returns the data it was provided with (optionally filling in the NAs)
head(fortify(pca))
# but you can provide the original data to fortify and it uses that
head(fortify(pca, data=d))
# then you can use columns in the original data to map aesthetics
autoplot(pca)
autoplot(pca, data=d, type="obs", mapping=aes(colour=foo, size=bar))

# the problem in using this in ggplot is that the data argument of ggplot() conflicts with the data argument of fortify()
ggplot(pca, data=d) + geom_point(aes(x=.PC1, y=.PC2, colour=foo))
# Results in:
# Error in ggplot.data.frame(pca, data = d) :
# Mapping should be created with aes or aes_string
# probably because .PC1 and .PC2 do not exist in d

# so you have to use fortify explicitly
ggplot(fortify(pca, data=d)) + geom_point(aes(x=.PC1, y=.PC2, colour=foo))
# but hopefully, autoplot is versatile enough to fit your needs (you can specify additional mappings and add layers with autoplot() + geom_***

The only cases that are not covered at the moment are:
- when there are NAs in the original data, that you want to impute them using iterative PCA *and* concatenate that with the *other* columns of the original data. pca() with completeObs=T would return the imputed data.frame but without the additional columns. Use data= in fortify would return the data with the NAs. In that case, you have to use completeObs() outside of pca() and do the rbinding with the other columns yourself.
- if you want to use a subset of rows in the pca() and still get all the original data. that currently fails at the rbind stage

In both cases I'm thinking that this could be a solution:

pcaData <- model@completeObs
# add the extracted columns: .PC1, .PC2, .cos2 etc.
# ...

origData <- data # provided through the data argument

# considering that both are non-NULL

commonCols <- names(origData) %in% names(pcaData)
origData <- origData[!commonCols]

# row names are conserved through the PCA (they are important because they usually are the observation identifier. They are used as labels in the plot) so we can do:
pcaData$.id <- row.names(pcaData)
origData$.id <- row.names(origData)
library("plyr")
join(origData, pcaData, by=".id", type="full")

This way:
- when pcaData has only a subset of rows compared to origData, the columns fetched from it (.PC1, .PC2 etc. but also the columns of the original data used to compute the PCA) have the missing lines filled with NAs by join with type="full"
- when the original data has NAs in the columns used to compute the pca(), those are imputed and used in the output
- when the original data has additional columns, they are concatenated with the rest, ensuring that the lines match (thanks to join).

So that only leaves us with a problem if the data used for the PCA is a subset of the lines of original, has NAs in that subset that you want to be filled, and that you want to make a plot with the original data except for the filled NAs. But I think this is enough of a corner case to forget about ;)

What do you think?

PS: additional questions:

- would it still be time to change fortify's interface to be :
fortify(model, orig.data, ...)
to avoid the conflict with the data argument of ggplot?

- how to use join() without having to explicitly load plyr when doing library("autoplot")? I guess that has something to do with importing the namespace or something but I am very unfamiliar with all this

- ideally, I should also not load ggplot explicity, but I am afraid this will be very complicated, and it's likely most people will need ggplot anyway so I lean of still loading it explicitly. What do you think?

Thanks in advance for the advice.

On 2012-Jul-07, at 14:24 , Brandon Hurr wrote:
>
>> So that only leaves us with a problem if the data used for the PCA is a subset of the lines of original, has NAs in that subset that you want to be filled, and that you want to make a plot with the original data except for the filled NAs. But I think this is enough of a corner case to forget about ;)
> This would be a very freak occurrence I think. If you do completeObs=T you lose the rows with NAs so you wouldn't likely ever run into the first two things together. Also, it's my understanding that pcaMethods::pca() won't fill in NAs in the original data, only in the .PC1 .PC2 data output from the PCA analysis would be imputed.

Actually, I think you are mistaken regarding completeObs. My (very short) testing suggests that completeObs=TRUE means impute the missing values through iterative PCA and return the full data with missing values imputed. See
?pca
...
completeObs: Sets the ‘completeObs’ slot on the resulting ‘pcaRes’
object containing the original data with but with all NAs
replaced with the estimates.
...

So, for example:
d <- data.frame(a=runif(10), b=runif(10), c=runif(10), foo=letters[round(runif(10, 1, 3))], bar=runif(10))

# add an NA
d[1,2] <- NA

library("pcaMethods")
library("autoplot")

# do not complete obs
pca <- pca(d[1:3], mode="svd", completeObs=F)
# pca@completeObs is NULL so
head(fortify(pca, type="obs"), 3)
# does not return any data, only the PCs and associated quantities
# but one can still supply the data to have it cbinded with those quantities
head(fortify(pca, type="obs", data=d), 3)

# now, complete obs
pca <- pca(d[1:3], mode="svd", completeObs=T)
# now pca@completeObs contains the imputed data
pca@completeObs
# and we use that in fortify
head(fortify(pca, type="obs"), 3)
# supplying the data replaces it
head(fortify(pca, type="obs", data=d), 3)

The behaviour I want to change is the last one: instead of replacing the data that comes from the PCA (the one with missing values filled) fortify should just supplement it with the additional columns foo and bar. This way, all possibilities would be covered (if you really want the data with NAs just use completeObs=FALSE).

One thing I am not sure about is how pca() treats missing values when completeObs=FALSE. It seems to me that it still does the imputation and computes the pca on the complete data afterwards, because it still outputs PCs for the lines with NAs and they as the same as when completeObs=TRUE, only, it does not return the imputed data.
I guess if the user really wants the NAs removed, he can always use na.omit() on the data fed to pca() but the choice of automatically imputing data is a surprising one, since you usually want the functions to let you know that there were NAs when they are there. An explicit option might be preferable.

As a side note: the code for pca() shows that when method=svd and that there are missing values, the method is switched to nipals automatically, without informing the user. A warning() or a message() would be in order I would think.

>> What do you think?
>>
>> PS: additional questions:
>>
>> - would it still be time to change fortify's interface to be :
>> fortify(model, orig.data, ...)
>> to avoid the conflict with the data argument of ggplot?
>
> Isn't it already?
> ?fortify
> Usage
> fortify(model, data, ...)
What I am suggesting is to change the name of the argument from "data" to "orig.data", to avoid conflicts.
